bugs: The rate limiter is set to Limit::perSecond(10) (app/Providers/AppServiceProvider.php:24). Laravel's limiter uses fixed windows, so up to about 20 jobs can start within any 1-second span that crosses a window boundary. That breaks the provider's 10 requests/second cap.

There is no atomic claim on the event. handle() only skips events already marked Processed (app/Jobs/ProcessWebhookEvent.php:54), so a second or duplicate job for an event marked Failed processes it again. A probe confirmed this: a Failed event run again ended up Processed. Duplicate jobs can come from webhooks:redispatch-stuck when the queue has a backlog.
Unknown event types are marked processed without being stored as failed or checked (ProcessWebhookEvent.php:60-63). This is defensible, but such events never become visible to admins.
A payment_id sent as an integer fails validation as 'string' and becomes a permanent failure (a probe confirmed this). This is an edge case.
antipatterns: app/Jobs/ProcessWebhookEvent.php:106 uses a match arm with `markPaid() && notify()` purely for its side effects; notify() returns void.
app/Jobs/ProcessWebhookEvent.php:32 keeps event types in a string array plus string match arms instead of a backed enum.
app/Notifications/PaymentReceipt.php:13 implements both ShouldQueue and ShouldQueueAfterCommit, which is redundant because the second extends the first.
app/Models/Order.php:78 transitionTo() runs a raw update that does not bump updated_at, and it calls refresh() even when nothing changed.
app/Models/Order.php:57 uses firstOrCreate for the refund even though there is a unique index; createOrFirst would be race-safe.
README.md keeps the stock Laravel boilerplate and adds the task docs at the bottom.
app/Payments/PaymentsClient.php:21 always sends a Bearer token, even an empty one.
strengths: The controller is thin: createOrFirst on a unique event_id, and the job is dispatched only when wasRecentlyCreated is true.
Uses WithoutOverlapping keyed per event, RateLimited, the Backoff/MaxExceptions/Timeout attributes, retryUntil, and failed() to mark events failed.
Handles 429/5xx/4xx correctly; 429 honours Retry-After through release.
Event payload data is validated per type; refund requires refund_id and amount.
Order state transitions use conditional updates, so they are idempotent, and a payment.failed arriving after payment does not downgrade the order.
Uses MassPrunable on processed_at, with model:prune scheduled daily, plus recovery of stuck events.
The README covers production workers well: Supervisor, --tries=0, retry_after ordering and queue:restart.
Tests include an end-to-end HTTP-to-queue test and a test that drives the real RateLimited middleware.

bugs: webhooks:redispatch-stale re-queues every event still marked Received after 15 minutes. That includes jobs that are only waiting in a backlog or were released by the rate limiter, so the queue fills with duplicate jobs under load. The atomic claim makes them harmless, but it is wasteful.
A non-string data.payment_id, such as an integer, is treated as missing and the event fails permanently (a probe confirmed this). This is an edge case.
Unknown event types fail only after an unnecessary call to the provider API (app/Actions/ApplyWebhookEvent.php:20 runs after api->payment).
antipatterns: app/Models/Order.php:65 uses a raw query update for the state transition and has to set updated_at by hand. It is acceptable for atomicity but bypasses model events.
The Action, the Service and the PermanentWebhookFailure exception add some extra layers for a small domain.
tests/Feature/ProcessWebhookEventTest.php:168 reads the Backoff attribute through reflection, which tests configuration rather than behaviour.
app/Jobs/ProcessWebhookEvent.php:24 includes the WithoutRelations attribute, which has no effect here.
strengths: The job claims the event atomically (a conditional update from Received/Processing to Processing), so failed or processed events are never run again even by duplicate jobs.

Uses WithoutOverlapping per event, RateLimited at 5/s with an explicit reason (fixed windows keep any 1-second span under 10/s), Backoff, MaxExceptions, Timeout, retryUntil and DeleteWhenMissingModels.
Domain work runs inside DB::transaction, and the receipt implements ShouldQueueAfterCommit and is sent only when the transition is won.
Uses createOrFirst for both events and refunds against unique indexes.
failed() refuses to overwrite a Processed event.
MassPrunable plus a scheduled model:prune; the README covers deployment thoroughly (Supervisor, shared cache, timeout ordering, Retry-After, restart on deploy, single scheduler).
Uses Sanctum with a policy via ->can(), a FormRequest with Rule::enum, and an API Resource that leaves out the payload.

The suite is broad: behavioural tests that the rate limiter releases events over the limit, that a held overlap lock blocks the job, a 5xx followed by success, 429 handled through withFakeQueueInteractions, plus Http::preventStrayRequests across the suite.

v.rationale:
I ranked impl-2 first. Both implementations pass their own suites (49 tests for impl-2, 42 for impl-1) and use similar modern patterns: createOrFirst intake, WithoutOverlapping plus RateLimited, Backoff/MaxExceptions/retryUntil, failed(), ShouldQueueAfterCommit receipts, MassPrunable, and a scheduled redispatch of stuck events.

impl-2 is ahead on correctness in three ways. First, it claims each event atomically, so an event already marked failed or processed is never run again; my probe confirmed that impl-1 re-runs a Failed event to Processed. Second, it sets the rate limit to 5/s on purpose so that fixed-window limiting stays under the provider's 10/s cap. impl-1's 10/s fixed window can allow about 20 requests in one second when bursts straddle a window boundary. Third, it guards failed() against overwriting a Processed event.

impl-2's README is focused and complete, while impl-1 adds its docs below the stock Laravel boilerplate. impl-2's tests also check queue behaviour more thoroughly.

impl-1 is somewhat simpler, validates the payload for each event type, and includes a good end-to-end test. Against that, it identifies event types with plain strings, uses firstOrCreate for refunds, and has a match arm that exists only for its side effects.

Both share a few small edge cases: an uppercase-hex signature is rejected, and an integer payment_id becomes a permanent failure.
